clue.text: Critic reveals the righteous at cathedral town

parts.note: the righteous, the holy ones, are saints
Bury St Edmunds in Suffolk is a cathedral town, shortened to Bury

explanation.surface: A reviewer exposes the pious folk of a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: George Saintsbury was a prolific English literary critic and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: George Saintsbury was a celebrated Victorian and Edwardian literary critic and historian of literature.

clue.text: Location of The Vision, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that a word is said aloud and a soundalike is written

parts.note: a vision is a sight, something seen

explanation.surface: Asking where a famous visionary work is set, as rumour has it.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a place or position, a synonym for location.

clue.text: Fateful date viewed from inside senate

indicators.note: viewed from tells us the letters are seen within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Caesar's doomed day as seen by someone inside the Roman senate.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March, 15 March, was the day Julius Caesar was murdered in the senate.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ides of March was the date of Caesar's assassination, foretold by a soothsayer as fatal.

clue.text: Deviously we hinder tether needed for Thurber's game

indicators.note: deviously means by roundabout routes, so the letters take a twisting new order

parts.note: the fodder as meant is 'we hide tether', whose twelve letters rearrange exactly

explanation.surface: Someone sneakily hampers a tethered animal that James Thurber's story requires.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, 'hinder' carries a spare N and R; the setter evidently meant 'hide'. Thurber's fairy tale The White Deer (1945) concerns a hunted deer, and 'game' means quarry, not a pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Thurber's book is about a deer pursued in a hunt, and hunted animals are called game.

clue.text: Noble novelist who suggested we should read all about it

definitions.text: Noble novelist who suggested we should read all about it

parts.words: Noble novelist who suggested we should read all about it
parts.note: a life peer who writes novels, and whose surname sounds like boasting, the very thing that urges us to read all about it

explanation.surface: A titled author who once urged the public to read every word about something.
explanation.walkthrough: Melvyn Bragg is a novelist and broadcaster made a life peer, Lord Bragg; to brag is to boast, inviting others to read all about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Melvyn Bragg, Lord Bragg of Wigton, is a peer and the author of many novels.

clue.text: Neruda's dwelling here below

parts.note: Pablo Neruda's poetry collection known in English as a home on Earth, here below meaning in this world

explanation.surface: Where the Chilean poet Neruda lived on this earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Neruda's Residencia en la tierra translates as Residence on Earth; 'here below' is an old phrase for earthly life.
explanation.definitionFit: A residence is a home or dwelling place, and the word heads the English title of Neruda's collection.

clue.text: Exchange at the start of some work about Proust

indicators.note: at the start of tells us to take the opening letter of each of the next words

explanation.surface: A trade made at the beginning of some study of Proust.
explanation.definitionFit: To swap is to trade one thing for another, an exchange.

clue.text: Slogans of McGough

parts.note: Roger McGough's 1969 poetry collection is titled with a word for rallying cries or mottos

explanation.surface: The catchphrases coined by the Liverpool poet Roger McGough.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger McGough, a Liverpool poet, published a collection called Watchwords in 1969.
explanation.definitionFit: Watchwords are mottos or rallying slogans, and the word names McGough's collection.

clue.text: Reading with difficulty about Foster's old dog showing

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes around the other

parts.note: poring is studying a text closely and laboriously
Stephen Foster's song is Old Dog Tray

explanation.surface: Laboriously reading about a dog from a Foster song while it is on display.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Foster, the American songwriter, wrote the sentimental song Old Dog Tray (1853); 'about' puts the dog inside the word for laborious reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Portraying is depicting or representing, which is showing something.

clue.text: Restoration architect's deterioration

definitions.meaning: John Vanbrugh, architect of Blenheim, wrote a Restoration comedy titled this
a falling back into illness or bad ways after improvement

explanation.surface: A Restoration-era architect's decline.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir John Vanbrugh, architect of Blenheim Palace, wrote the comedy The Relapse (1696).
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a slide back into worse health or habits, a deterioration.

clue.text: Child of Frederik Pohl

parts.note: Frederik Pohl and Jack Williamson wrote a science-fiction novel whose title is this word followed by child

explanation.surface: A son or daughter of the science-fiction writer Frederik Pohl.
explanation.walkthrough: Starchild (1965) is a novel by Frederik Pohl and Jack Williamson, so this word comes before 'child'.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel title Starchild is this celestial body joined to the word child.

clue.text: A curt satiric version from Cruikshank

indicators.note: a version is a rendering in another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A short, sharp satirical piece by the illustrator George Cruikshank.
explanation.walkthrough: George Cruikshank was a celebrated 19th-century English satirical cartoonist who illustrated Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Cruikshank drew exaggerated satirical portraits, making him a famous example of a cartoonist of that kind.

clue.text: Puzo's sponsor

definitions.meaning: Mario Puzo's best-known novel about a Mafia family
one who sponsors a child at baptism

explanation.surface: Mario Puzo's backer.
explanation.definitionFit: A godparent sponsors a child at christening; Puzo's novel takes its title from the Mafia boss called this.

clue.text: The part-time typist estimated by Shadwell

parts.note: a temp is a temporary office worker such as a typist
est. is the abbreviation for estimated

explanation.surface: A temporary secretary whose worth was assessed by someone named Shadwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Shadwell adapted Shakespeare's play as a semi-opera in 1674.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadwell produced an operatic adaptation of Shakespeare's storm play, so it is a work by him.

clue.text: "We wandered through Marie Antoinette ——' —" (The Great Gatsby)

definitions.text: "We wandered through Marie Antoinette ——' —" (The Great Gatsby)

parts.words: "We wandered through Marie Antoinette ——' —" (The Great Gatsby)
parts.note: the missing words in Fitzgerald's line name rooms for playing and hearing performances, paired with Restoration salons

explanation.surface: A quotation from The Great Gatsby with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitzgerald's line runs: 'We wandered through Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration salons'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gatsby's mansion has rooms for playing instruments, which is the phrase missing from the quotation.

clue.text: Highly prized author whose work featured a sunken bell

definitions.text: Highly prized author whose work featured a sunken bell

parts.words: Highly prized author whose work featured a sunken bell
parts.note: a German Nobel prizewinner whose verse drama Die versunkene Glocke tells of a bell lost in a lake

explanation.surface: A much-valued writer whose work includes a bell that went under.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerhart Hauptmann won the 1912 Nobel Prize for Literature ('highly prized'); his play The Sunken Bell dates from 1896.
explanation.definitionFit: Gerhart Hauptmann, Nobel laureate, wrote the fairy-tale drama The Sunken Bell.

clue.text: "Like all — things, he quicker flies / The place approaching …" (Crabbe)

definitions.text: "Like all — things, he quicker flies / The place approaching …" (Crabbe)

parts.words: "Like all — things, he quicker flies / The place approaching …" (Crabbe)
parts.note: the gap in George Crabbe's couplet is a word for things drawn toward something, speeding as they near

explanation.surface: A gapped couplet from the poet George Crabbe.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word describes things pulled by a force that grows as they near its source.
explanation.definitionFit: Objects drawn by a pull move faster as they near it, which fits the gap in Crabbe's couplet.

clue.text: One among life's little ones from Hardy?

definitions.text: One among life's little ones from Hardy?

parts.words: One among life's little ones from Hardy?
parts.note: Thomas Hardy's story collection is Life's Little Ironies, so one of the little ones is a single example

explanation.surface: One of the small children in Thomas Hardy's life.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's 1894 short-story collection is Life's Little Ironies; 'little ones' seems to mean children.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's collection title refers to small mocking twists of fate, of which this is one.

clue.text: It identifies Frank Norris's circle

parts.note: Frank Norris's story collection is The ___ Circle, and the missing ordinal word identifies which circle

explanation.surface: Something that pins down the social set of the American novelist Frank Norris.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank Norris's posthumous collection is The Third Circle (1909); 'circle' looks like his social group.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norris's title The Third Circle the ordinal number is the word that tells which circle is meant.

clue.text: Where Marvell fell on grass

parts.note: in Andrew Marvell's poem the speaker, ensnared with flowers, falls on grass; the clue asks the poem's title, the place of the fall

explanation.surface: The spot where the poet Andrew Marvell took a tumble onto the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Marvell's poem The Garden has the line 'Insnared with flowers, I fall on grass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvell's poem is set among flowers and fruit in a cultivated plot, the scene of his fall.

clue.text: Ruth dreamt, or made up, death of king

indicators.note: made up means invented or put together, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Ruth had a dream, or else invented, the death of a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur tells of King Arthur's death; 'morte' is French for death.
explanation.definitionFit: Malory's title means the death of Arthur, the legendary king of Britain.

clue.text: Nobleman's article about article

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is nobleman

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes around the second

parts.note: the definite article in English is the
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A grammatical point about one article written about another.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland a thane was a clan chief or lord, like Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A thane was an Anglo-Saxon or Scottish lord holding land from the king, a nobleman.

clue.text: Nothing to spoil mathematician-poet

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
to mar is to spoil or damage

explanation.surface: No need to ruin the reputation of a poet who was also a mathematician.
explanation.walkthrough: Omar Khayyam, the Persian poet of the Rubaiyat, was also a noted mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: Omar Khayyam was a Persian mathematician and astronomer famed for his quatrains.

clue.text: One little sibling for goddess

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
sis is a short form of sister

explanation.surface: A single younger sister fit to be a goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Isis was the chief goddess of ancient Egypt, wife of Osiris.

clue.text: Cupid gets sore back

indicators.note: back means read backwards, so the letters of sore are turned round

explanation.surface: The god of love develops an aching back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a body part to go with 'sore'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, counterpart of the Roman Cupid.

clue.text: Morton's doctor's squint

definitions.meaning: J.B. Morton's Beachcomber column featured the absurd scientist Dr ___ (Whom God Preserve) of Utrecht

explanation.surface: A physician from a writer's column has a cross-eyed look.
explanation.walkthrough: J.B. Morton wrote the 'Beachcomber' humour column in the Daily Express, featuring Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve) of Utrecht.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabismus is the medical name for a squint, eyes not lining up.

clue.text: River of The Trial

definitions.meaning: a chalk stream in Hampshire famous for trout fishing
a trial is a ... or examination

explanation.surface: A river that features in Kafka's novel The Trial.
explanation.walkthrough: The Test is a Hampshire river in southern England; 'The Trial' looks like Kafka's novel but simply means a trial.
explanation.definitionFit: A test is a trial of quality or ability; the Test is also a river in Hampshire.

clue.text: Those of Philip reintroduce us to Arthur Pendennis

definitions.text: Those of Philip reintroduce us to Arthur Pendennis

parts.words: Those of Philip reintroduce us to Arthur Pendennis
parts.note: Thackeray's last novel, about Philip's exploits on his way through the world, is narrated by Arthur Pendennis, hero of an earlier book

explanation.surface: Philip's escapades bring back Thackeray's character Arthur Pendennis.
explanation.walkthrough: Thackeray's The Adventures of Philip (1862) is narrated by Arthur Pendennis, the hero of his earlier Pendennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's novel title speaks of Philip's exploits, his escapades on his way through the world.
